a.text: Which part of the thoracic spinal nerve contains preganglionic sympathetic fibers?
a.explanation: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers leave the spinal cord through ventral roots.
a.keyConcept: Thoracic Spinal Nerves: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers leave the spinal cord through ventral roots

b.text: Which part of the thoracic spinal nerve that contains preganglionic sympathetic fibers?
b.explanation: The correct answer is the Ventral root because preganglionic sympathetic axons leave the lateral horn with the somatic motor fibres and then pass to the sympathetic chain through the white ramus communicans. The grey ramus carries postganglionic, not preganglionic, fibres back to the spinal nerve. The dorsal root and its ganglion are sensory.
b.keyConcept: Preganglionic sympathetic fibres exit in the ventral root and reach the chain via the white ramus communicans.

a.text: The circulation that begins from capillaries and ends into capillaries:
a.explanation: A portal system connects two capillary beds in series.
a.keyConcept: Portal Circulation: A portal system connects two capillary beds in series

b.text: The circulation that begins from capillaries & ends into capillaries is called:
b.explanation: The correct answer is Portal because a portal system starts in one capillary bed and ends in a second capillary or sinusoidal bed without passing through the heart in between. The hepatic portal vein and the hypophyseal portal system are the two classic examples. The systemic and pulmonary circuits both begin and end at the heart.
b.keyConcept: A portal system links two capillary beds in series.

a.text: The parasagittal plane divides the body into:
a.explanation: The correct answer is right & left unequal halves because a parasagittal plane is any vertical antero-posterior plane parallel to, but not through, the midline. Only the median (mid-sagittal) plane gives equal right and left halves. Anterior/posterior division is the coronal plane and upper/lower division is the transverse plane.
a.keyConcept: Median plane = equal halves; parasagittal = unequal right and left parts.

b.text: A parasagittal plane divides the body into:
b.explanation: A parasagittal plane runs parallel to the median plane but away from the midline, producing unequal right and left portions.
b.keyConcept: Median plane gives equal halves; parasagittal planes give unequal portions.

a.text: Most of the joints that lie in the median plane of the body are:
a.explanation: The correct answer is Secondary cartilaginous joint because symphyses are characteristically midline structures: the symphysis pubis, the intervertebral discs and the manubriosternal joint. Primary cartilaginous joints such as epiphyseal plates are not confined to the midline. Syndesmoses and gomphoses are fibrous joints found elsewhere.
a.keyConcept: Midline joints are typically secondary cartilaginous (symphyses).

b.text: Most joints that lie in the median plane of the body are:
b.explanation: Secondary cartilaginous joints, or symphyses, characteristically lie in the midline, as at the symphysis pubis, intervertebral discs, and manubriosternal joint.
b.keyConcept: Midline joints are commonly secondary cartilaginous symphyses.

a.text: Which part of the spinal nerve is formed of purely motor fibers?
a.explanation: The correct answer is the Ventral root because it contains the axons of the anterior horn cells, together with preganglionic autonomic fibres in the appropriate segments. The dorsal root is purely sensory, and the nerve trunk and both rami are mixed after the roots join.
a.keyConcept: The ventral root carries motor axons from anterior horn cells out of the cord.

b.text: Which part of a spinal nerve is formed of purely motor fibers?
b.explanation: The ventral root carries motor axons away from the spinal cord. The dorsal root is sensory, while the spinal nerve trunk and both rami are mixed.
b.keyConcept: Ventral root = motor; dorsal root = sensory; rami = mixed.

a.text: Which ventral rami that do not form nerve plexuses?
a.explanation: The correct answer is the Thoracic rami because the ventral rami of T2 to T11 run independently as intercostal nerves and retain a strictly segmental distribution. The cervical, lumbar and sacral rami interlace to form the cervical, brachial, lumbar and sacral plexuses, and the coccygeal ramus joins the small coccygeal plexus.
a.keyConcept: Thoracic ventral rami stay segmental as intercostal nerves and form no plexus.

b.text: Which ventral rami do not form nerve plexuses?
b.explanation: Thoracic ventral rami remain segmental as intercostal and subcostal nerves rather than interlacing to form a plexus.
b.keyConcept: Thoracic ventral rami generally do not form plexuses.

a.text: An example of an anatomical end artery:
a.explanation: The correct answer is the Central retinal artery because it has no anastomosis whatsoever with neighbouring arteries, so its occlusion causes immediate and total blindness of that eye. The coronary and cerebral arteries are functional end arteries, having anastomoses that are too small to be effective. The mesenteric and renal arteries have richer connections.
a.keyConcept: Anatomical end artery = no anastomosis at all: central artery of the retina.

b.text: An example of an anatomical end artery is:
b.explanation: The central retinal artery has no effective anastomosis and is a true anatomical end artery. Coronary and cerebral arteries are generally described as functional end arteries because their anastomoses are inadequate.
b.keyConcept: The central retinal artery is an anatomical end artery.

a.text: Amino acids are ampholytes because they can function as either a(n):
a.explanation: Amino acids contain proton-accepting amino groups and proton-donating carboxyl groups, enabling acid and base behavior.

b.text: Amino acids are ampholytes because they can function as either an):
b.explanation: Amino and carboxyl groups permit amino acids to accept or donate protons, so they function as bases or acids.

a.text: There are four parts to each amino acid. A carbon atom is bonded to a hydrogen atom, R group, and functional groups are : 6
a.explanation: The alpha carbon of a typical amino acid bears an amino group, a carboxyl group, hydrogen and an R group.

b.text: There are four parts to each amino acid. A carbon atom is bonded to a hydrogen atom, R group, and functional groups are :
b.explanation: A typical alpha carbon is attached to amino and carboxyl functional groups plus hydrogen and the variable R group.

a.text: All of the following are polar amino acids Except:
a.explanation: Alanine has a methyl side chain; glutamate and arginine are charged and serine is polar through its hydroxyl group.

b.text: AlI of the following are polar amino acids Except:
b.explanation: Alanine's methyl side chain is nonpolar; glutamate and arginine are charged and serine is hydroxyl-bearing and polar.

a.text: Serine is important in the structure of some proteins as it provide which of the following groups?
a.explanation: Serine's side-chain hydroxyl supports hydrogen bonding and can serve as a phosphorylation site.

b.text: Serine is important for the function of some proteins since it provides which of these groups?
b.explanation: Serine has a side-chain hydroxyl that can participate in catalysis and phosphorylation.

a.text: Which amino acid can form disulphide bonds?
a.explanation: Oxidation of two cysteine thiols creates a disulfide crosslink; the other listed residues lack thiols.

b.text: Which amine acid can form disulphide bonds
b.explanation: Cysteine thiols oxidize in pairs to produce disulfide bridges; the other listed side chains lack thiols.

a.explanation: Peptide bonds establish the primary backbone; tertiary folding is stabilized by side-chain interactions including hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic effects and disulfides.

b.text: The tertiary structure of proteins is stabilized by all the following EXCEPT:
b.explanation: Peptide bonds determine the primary chain sequence; hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions and disulfides stabilize tertiary folding.

a.text: The two-subunit (dimer) structure of creatine kinase represents which level of protein structure?
a.explanation: Association of two polypeptide chains is quaternary structure, regardless of each individual chain's tertiary fold.

b.text: The two-subunit (Dimmer) structure of the Creatine kinase represents protein's:
b.explanation: Association of two polypeptide subunits is quaternary structure; tertiary structure describes each chain individually.

a.text: One of the following is true concerning fibrous protein: 8

b.text: One of the following is true concerning fibrous protein:

a.explanation: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is caused by deficient pulmonary surfactant, whose major surface-active phospholipid is dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (dipalmitoyl lecithin).

a.text: Which of the following is not formed during the Krebs cycle?
a.explanation: Lactate is formed by reduction of pyruvate outside the TCA cycle. Isocitrate, succinate and oxaloacetate are intermediates of the cycle itself.

b.text: Which is not formed during the Krebs cycle?

a.text: Characters of homeostasis control mechanism are:
a.explanation: A homeostatic control system classically includes sensors that detect change, an integrating center that compares the value with the set point, and effectors that produce the corrective response. Therefore all of the listed components are part of the mechanism.
a.keyConcept: Homeostatic loops require sensors, a control center, and effectors.

b.text: characters of homestasis control mechanism are:
b.explanation: Homeostatic control mechanisms require a detector, a controller, and a responder. Sensors detect the change, the integrating center interprets it, and effectors carry out the corrective action, so all are included.
b.keyConcept: Homeostatic control needs sensing, integration, and action.

a.text: Number of osmoles/liter of solution is called:
a.explanation: Osmolarity is defined as the number of osmoles per liter of solution. Osmolality is per kilogram of solvent, and tonicity refers to the effect on cell volume.

b.text: Number of Osmoles/ liters of solution is called:
b.explanation: Osmoles per litre of solution defines osmolarity, while osmoles per kilogram of solvent defines osmolality. Tonicity is a different idea again, describing only the effective osmoles, those that cannot cross the membrane and can therefore actually shift water. Urea illustrates the distinction, since it adds to measured osmolarity but, because it penetrates cells, contributes almost nothing to tonicity.
b.keyConcept: Osmolarity counts all solute per litre, while tonicity counts only the impermeant solute that can move water.

a.text: Turbulence becomes evident if Reynold number exceeds:
a.explanation: Reynolds number expresses the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in a flowing fluid. Small values such as 100 or 200 are firmly laminar, and although instability can begin around 2000, turbulence becomes clearly evident once the number exceeds about 3000.
a.keyConcept: Turbulence becomes clearly evident above a Reynolds number of about 3000.

b.text: Turbulence becomes evident if Raynald’s number exceeds
b.explanation: Reynolds number weighs inertial against viscous forces, Re = density x velocity x diameter / viscosity. Below about 2000 flow is reliably laminar, between 2000 and 3000 it is transitional, and above 3000 turbulence is frankly established. Turbulence matters clinically twice over: it wastes energy, so a much larger pressure gradient is needed for the same flow, and it generates the vibrations heard as bruits and murmurs.
b.keyConcept: Laminar below about 2000, transitional between 2000 and 3000, clearly turbulent above 3000.

b.explanation: Interphase comprises G1, S, and G2. G1 supports growth and preparation for replication, S duplicates DNA, G2 prepares for division, and M includes mitosis and cytokinesis; G0 is entered from G1.

a.text: What diagnostic tool will you use to diagnose Down Syndrome?
a.explanation: Karyotyping evaluates chromosome number and large structural changes in dividing nucleated cells. Earlier mitotic arrest improves banding resolution. Microarray detects copy-number imbalance but generally misses balanced translocations.

a.text: The RNA with a high percentage of modified nucleotides is:
a.explanation: tRNA is the amino-acid adaptor: its anticodon pairs with an mRNA codon, while the amino acid is ester-linked to the terminal adenosine of its 3′-CCA end. Its folded structure contains internal base pairs and numerous modified bases.

a.text: When a charged tRNA approaches the ribosome during elongation, it enters the large ribosomal subunit at the:
a.explanation: Initiator tRNA occupies the P site. During elongation, incoming charged tRNA enters A, peptide transfer leaves the growing chain on A-site tRNA, and translocation moves it to P while empty tRNA moves to E. A stop codon in A recruits a release factor that hydrolyzes the P-site peptidyl-tRNA bond.

a.text: The alternate forms of a gene are called:
a.explanation: Homozygous means identical alleles at a locus; heterozygous means different alleles. A compound heterozygote has two different pathogenic alleles of the same gene.
